newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal pay talks resume in Hesse region.
newsitem.headline: German metal pay talks resume in Hesse region.

text.p: German metal and engineering workers resumed 1997 pay talks with employers in the Hesse region, just hours after their colleagues in the southern region of Nordwuerttemberg restarted similar talks.

The IG Metall union and employers restarted talks for the Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saar region. Union chief negotiator Karl-Guenther Kronawitter said the group would only accept an agreement that matched those reached elsewhere.

German wage negotiations in various industries have been pulled forward by several months as workers threatened protests after a new German law allowed companies to reduce salaries during illness to 80 percent.

In Hesse, employer group chief negotiator Heinrich Fischer said the two sides were still far apart and that an agreement for the region's 400,000 workers could not be necessarily expected at the end of today's second round of talks.

The union had managed to secure assurances that employers would continue to pay full salaries during illness, even though companies are now allowed to reduce payments to 80 percent in a bid to cut costs.
But the union has made no concessions to the employers yet.
Earlier in the day metal and engineering workers restarted 1997 pay talks with employers in the southern region of Nordwuerttemberg after Tuesday's failure to reach agreement on sick payments.

Following mass protests and the threat of strikes in the already hard-hit industry, most of Germany's engineering firms have now backed away from enshrining the law in worker contracts and instead agreed to cut labour costs in other ways.

In Nordwuerttemberg, where some 600,000 are employed in the sector, employers are still holding out for tougher terms than those secured in other sectoral pay deals across the country, all of which have secured sick pat at 100 percent.
Klaus Fritsche, chief negotiator for the employers' side, said going into the talks that they would "negotiate constructively".
But union officials, which had earlier this week been confident of a deal, said they were not making any forecasts on how the talks would progress.
Meanwhile wage talks in the German construction industry also began in Frankfurt but were also not expected to reach agreement today.
The union IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt has said one of its key objectives is to battle seasonal unemployment which soared to 400,00 workers last winter.
"We will not even come close to nearing an agreement today," Klaus Wiesehuegel, head of the union said.
